arXiv:1505.05525v2 [math.AP] 10 Mar 2016

Hölder gradient estimates for parabolic homogeneous pp-Laplacian equations

Tianling Jin Note: Supported in part by NSF grant DMS-1362525.    and    Luis Silvestre Note: Supported in part by NSF grants DMS-1254332 and DMS-1065979.
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We prove interior Hölder estimates for the spatial gradient of viscosity solutions to the parabolic homogeneous pp-Laplacian equation

ut=|∇u|2−p div(|∇u|p−2∇u),u_{t}=|\nabla u|^{2-p}\mbox{ div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u),

where 1<p<∞1<p<\infty. This equation arises from tug-of-war-like stochastic games with noise. It can also be considered as the parabolic pp-Laplacian equation in non divergence form.

1 Introduction

For 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, the pp-Laplacian equation

Δpu:= div(|∇u|p−2∇u)=0\Delta_{p}u:=\mbox{ div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u)=0 (1.1)

is the Euler-Lagrange equation of the energy functional

1p​∫|∇u​(x)|p​𝑑x,\frac{1}{p}\int|\nabla u(x)|^{p}dx, (1.2)

where ∇\nabla and div are the gradient and divergence operators in the variable x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. It is a classical result that every weak solution of (1.1) in the distribution sense is C1,αC^{1,\alpha} for some α>0\alpha>0. This result and its various proofs can be found in, e.g., Ural’ceva [50], Uhlenbeck [49], Evans [12], DiBenedetto [8], Lewis [34], Tolksdorf [48] and Wang [51].

The negative gradient flow of the energy functional (1.2) takes the form of

ut= div(|∇u|p−2∇u).u_{t}=\mbox{ div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u). (1.3)

Hölder estimates for the spatial gradient of weak solutions to (1.3) were obtained by DiBenedetto and Friedman in [10] (see also Wiegner [53]), and we refer to the book of DiBenedetto [9] for an extensive overview on (1.3) and more general cases.

The equation above comes from a variational interpretation of the pp-Laplacian operator. This is not the equation we study in this work. Our equation is motivated by the stochastic tug of war game interpretation of the pp-Laplacian operator given by Peres and Sheffield in [41]. Such time dependent stochastic games will lead not to (1.1), but rather the equation

ut=|∇u|2−p div(|∇u|p−2∇u).u_{t}=|\nabla u|^{2-p}\mbox{ div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u). (1.4)

This derivation is presented in Manfredi-Parviainen-Rossi [37]. The equation (1.4) can also be written as

ut=(δi​j+(p−2)​|∇u|−2​ui​uj)​ui​j,u_{t}=(\delta_{ij}+(p-2)|\nabla u|^{-2}u_{i}u_{j})u_{ij}, (1.5)

where the summation convention is used. Through (1.5), one can view the equation (1.4) as the parabolic pp-Laplacian equation in non divergence form.

The majority of the previous work on elliptic and parabolic pp-Laplace equation rely heavily on the variational structure of the equation. The equation (1.4) does not have that structure. Therefore, we must take a completely different point of view using tools for equations in non-divergence form. To begin with, our notion of solution would be a viscosity solution instead of a solution in the sense of distributions. Thus, this work has hardly anything in common with the more classical results about regularity for pp-Laplacian type equations. We use maximum principles and geometrical methods.

Our work concerns the equation (1.4) for the values of p∈(1,+∞)p\in(1,+\infty). In this case, the existence and uniqueness of viscosity solutions to the initial-boundary value problems for (1.4) have been established in Banerjee-Garofalo [1] and Does [11], where they also proved the Lipschitz continuity in the spatial variables and studied the long time behavior of the viscosity solution. These properties were further studied in [2, 3, 26] for (1.4) or more general equations. Manfredi, Parviainen and Rossi studied the equation (1.4) as an asymptotic limit of certain mean value properties which are related to the tug-of-war game with noise originally described in [41], when the number of rounds is bounded. One may find more results on the tug-of-war game with noise and the pp-Laplacian operators in, e.g., [28, 33, 36, 38, 42, 43, 44].

Even though all published work about the equation (1.4) appeared only in recent years, we have seen an unpublished handwritten note by N. Garofalo from 1993 referring to this equation. In that note, there is a computation which leads to the result of Lemma 3.1 in this paper. This is, up to our knowledge, the first time when it was recognized that the equation (1.4) should have good regularization properties.

It is interesting to point out what our equation represents for p=1p=1 and p=+∞p=+\infty, even though these end-point cases are not included in our analysis. They appeared in the literature much earlier than (1.4). In these two cases, it is clear that the parabolic equation in non-divergence form (1.4) is more important and better motivated than (1.3).

When p=1p=1, the equation (1.4) is the motion of the level sets of uu by its mean curvature, which has been studied by, e.g., Chen-Giga-Goto [6], Evans-Spruck [17, 18, 19, 20], Evans-Soner-Souganidis [16], Ishii-Souganidis [24] and Colding-Minicozzi [7]. A game of motion by mean curvature was introduced by Spencer [47] and studied by Kohn and Serfaty [29].

In another extremal case p=+∞p=+\infty, it becomes the evolution governed by the infinity Laplacian operator. The infinity Laplacian operator Δ∞\Delta_{\infty} defined by Δ∞​u=∑i,jui​ui​ui​j\Delta_{\infty}u=\sum_{i,j}u_{i}u_{i}u_{ij} appears naturally when one considers absolutely minimizing Lipschitz extensions of a function defined on the boundary of a domain. Jensen [25] proved that the absolute minimizer is the unique viscosity solution of the infinity Laplace equation Δ∞​u=0\Delta_{\infty}u=0, of which the solutions are usually called infinity harmonic functions. Savin in [45] has shown that infinity harmonic functions are in fact continuously differentiable in the two dimensional case, and Evans-Savin [14] further proved the Hölder continuity of their gradient. Later, Evans-Smart [15] proved the everywhere differentiability of infinity harmonic functions in all dimensions. A game theoretical interpretation of this infinity Laplacian was given by Peres-Schramm-Sheffield-Wilson [40]. Finite difference methods for the infinity Laplace and pp-Laplace equations were studied by Oberman [39]. The parabolic equation (1.4) in this extremal case p=∞p=\infty has been studied by, e.g., Juutinen-Kawohl [27] and Barron-Evans-Jensen [4].

Our notion of solutions to (1.5) is the viscosity solution, which will be recalled in Definition 2.8 in Section 2. For 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, one observes that

min⁡(p−1,1)​I≤δi​j+(p−2)​qi​qi​|q|−2≤max⁡(p−1,1)​Ifor all ​q∈ℝn∖{0},\min(p-1,1)I\leq\delta_{ij}+(p-2)q_{i}q_{i}|q|^{-2}\leq\max(p-1,1)I\quad\mbox{for all }q\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\},

where II is the n×nn\times n identity matrix. Therefore, the equation (1.5) is uniformly parabolic. It follows from the regularity theory of Krylov-Safonov [31] that the viscosity solution uu of (1.5) is Hölder continuous in the space-time variables. As mentioned earlier, Banerjee-Garofalo [1] and Does [11] proved that the solution uu is Lipschitz continuous in the spatial variables. Whether or not the spatial gradient ∇u\nabla u is Hölder continuous was left as an interesting open question.

In this paper, we answer this question and prove the following interior Hölder estimates for the spatial gradient of viscosity solutions to (1.5).

Theorem 1.1.

Let uu be a viscosity solution of (1.5) in Q1Q_{1}, where 1<p<∞1<p<\infty. Then there exist two constants α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and C>0C>0, both of which depends only on nn and pp, such that

‖∇u‖Cα​(Q1/2)≤C​‖u‖L∞​(Q1).\|\nabla u\|_{C^{\alpha}(Q_{1/2})}\leq C\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}.

Also, there holds

sup(x,t),(x,s)∈Q1/2|u⁡(x,t)−u⁡(x,s)||t−s|1+α2≤C​‖u‖L∞​(Q1).\sup_{(x,t),(x,s)\in Q_{1/2}}\frac{|u(x,t)-u(x,s)|}{|t-s|^{\frac{1+\alpha}{2}}}\leq C\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}.

Here, Qr=Br×(−r2,0]Q_{r}=B_{r}\times(-r^{2},0] is denoted as the standard parabolic cylinder, where r>0r>0 and Br⊂ℝnB_{r}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is the ball of radius rr centered at the origin. Combining those two estimates in Theorem 1.1, we have that

|u⁡(y,s)−u⁡(x,t)−∇u​(x,t)⋅(y−x)|≤C​‖u‖L∞​(Q1)​(|y−x|+|t−s|)1+α|u(y,s)-u(x,t)-\nabla u(x,t)\cdot(y-x)|\leq C\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}(|y-x|+\sqrt{|t-s|})^{1+\alpha}

for all (y,s),(x,t)∈Q1/2(y,s),(x,t)\in Q_{1/2}.

The equation (1.5) is quasi-linear, and (δi​j+(p−2)​|∇u|−2​ui​uj)(\delta_{ij}+(p-2)|\nabla u|^{-2}u_{i}u_{j}) can be viewed as the coefficients of the equation. Note that these coefficients have a singularity when ∇u=0\nabla u=0. This is what causes the main difficulties in the proof of our main result. The only thing in common with previous proofs of C1,αC^{1,\alpha} regularity with equations of pp-Laplacian type is perhaps the general outline of steps necessary for the proof. The oscillation of the gradient is reduced in a shrinking sequence of parabolic cylinders. The iterative step is reduced to a dichotomy between two cases: either the value of the gradient ∇u\nabla u stays close to a fixed vector ee for most points (x,t)(x,t) (in measure), or it does not. The way each of these two cases is resolved (which is the key of the proof), follows a new idea. Traditionally, the variational structure of the equation played a crucial role in the resolution of each of these two cases. The key ideas in this paper are contained in Section 4, especially in Lemmas 4.1 and 4.4. Lemma 4.4 allows us to apply a recent result by Yu Wang [52] (which is the parabolic version of a result by Savin [46]) to resolve one of the two cases in the dichotomy.

In the process of proving Lemma 4.4, we obtain Lemma 4.3 which is a general property of solutions to uniformly parabolic equations and may be interesting by itself. It states that an upper bound on the oscillation  oscx∈B1​u​(x,t)\mbox{ osc}_{x\in B_{1}}u(x,t) for every fixed t∈[a,b]t\in[a,b] implies an upper bound in space-time for  osc(x,t)∈B1×[a,b]​u​(x,t)\mbox{ osc}_{(x,t)\in B_{1}\times[a,b]}u(x,t).

In future work [22], we plan to adapt the method presented in this paper to obtain the Hölder continuity of ∇u\nabla u for the following generalization of (1.4):

ut=|∇u|κ​Δp​u.u_{t}=|\nabla u|^{\kappa}\Delta_{p}u.

Here κ\kappa is an arbitrary power in the range κ∈(1−p,+∞)\kappa\in(1-p,+\infty). The equation generalizes both the classical (scalar) parabolic pp-Laplacian equation in divergence form (1.3) and in non divergence form (1.4).

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we start by recalling some well-known regularity results for solutions of uniformly parabolic equations which will be used in our proof of Theorem 1.1, as well as the definition and two properties of the viscosity solutions of (1.5). We then introduce a regularization procedure for (1.5). In Section 3, we will establish Lipschitz estimates for the solutions uu of its regularized problem. The result of Section 3 is not new, but we present a new proof within our context. In Section 4, we obtain the Hölder estimates for ∇u\nabla u, which is the most technically challenging part and the core of this paper. Finally, Theorem 1.1 will follow from approximation arguments, whose details will be presented in Section 5.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we recall some known regularity results for solutions of linear uniformly parabolic equations with measurable coefficients:

ut−ai​j​(x,t)​∂i​ju=0 in ​Q1,u_{t}-a_{ij}(x,t)\partial_{ij}u=0\quad\text{ in }Q_{1}, (2.1)

where ai​j​(x,t)a_{ij}(x,t) is uniformly parabolic, i.e. there are constants 0<λ≤Λ<∞0<\lambda\leq\Lambda<\infty such that

λ​I≤ai​j​(x,t)≤Λ​I for all ​(x,t)∈Q1.\lambda I\leq a_{ij}(x,t)\leq\Lambda I\quad\text{ for all }(x,t)\in Q_{1}. (2.2)

The first two in the below are the weak Harnack inequality and local maximum principle due to Krylov and Safonov. For their proofs, we refer to the lecture notes by Imbert and Silvestre [23].

Theorem 2.1 (Weak Harnack inequality).

Let u∈C⁡(Q1)u\in C(Q_{1}) be a non negative supersolution of (2.1) satisfying (2.2). Then there exist two positive constants θ\theta (small) and CC (large), both of which depend only on n,λn,\lambda and Λ\Lambda, such that

‖u‖Lθ​(Q1/2∗)≤C​infQ1/2u,\|u\|_{L^{\theta}(Q^{*}_{1/2})}\leq C\inf_{Q_{1/2}}u,

where Q1/2∗=B1/2×(−1,−3/4)Q_{1/2}^{*}=B_{1/2}\times(-1,-3/4).

Theorem 2.2 (Local maximum principle).

Let u∈C⁡(Q1)u\in C(Q_{1}) be a subsolution of (2.1) satisfying (2.2). For every γ>0\gamma>0, there exists a positive constant CC depending only on γ,n,λ\gamma,n,\lambda and Λ\Lambda, such that

supQ1/2u≤C​‖u+‖Lγ​(Q1),\sup_{Q_{1/2}}u\leq C\|u^{+}\|_{L^{\gamma}(Q_{1})},

where u+=max⁡(u,0)u^{+}=\max(u,0).

The exact statement which we will use regarding to improvement of oscillation for supersolutions of (2.1) is of the following form.

Proposition 2.3 (Improvement of oscillation).

Let u∈C⁡(Q1)u\in C(Q_{1}) be a non negative supersolution of (2.1) satisfying (2.2). For every μ∈(0,1)\mu\in(0,1), there exist two positive constants τ\tau and γ\gamma, where τ\tau depends only on μ\mu and nn, and γ\gamma depends only on μ,n,λ\mu,n,\lambda and Λ\Lambda, such that if

then

A consequence of Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 2.2 is the following interior Hölder estimate by Krylov and Safonov [31].

Theorem 2.4 (Interior Hölder estimates).

Let u∈C⁡(Q1)u\in C(Q_{1}) be a solution of (2.1) satisfying (2.2). Then there exist two positive constants α\alpha (small) and CC (large), both of which depend only on n,λn,\lambda and Λ\Lambda, such that

‖u‖Cα​(Q1/2)≤C​ oscQ1​u\|u\|_{C^{\alpha}(Q_{1/2})}\leq C\mbox{ osc}_{Q_{1}}u

Here, we write  oscQ​u:=supQu−infQu\mbox{ osc}_{Q}\,u:=\sup_{Q}u-\inf_{Q}u. Note that by adding or subtracting an appropriate constant, the estimate in the previous theorem is equivalent to

‖u‖Cα​(Q1/2)≤C​‖u‖L∞​(Q1).\|u\|_{C^{\alpha}(Q_{1/2})}\leq C\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}.

Meanwhile, we shall also use a boundary regularity property. For two real numbers aa and bb, we denote

a∨b=max⁡(a,b),a∧b=min⁡(a,b).a\vee b=\max(a,b),\ a\wedge b=\min(a,b).

We also denote

∂pQr=(∂Br×(−r2,0))∪(Br×{(x,t):t=−r2})\partial_{p}Q_{r}=(\partial B_{r}\times(-r^{2},0))\cup(B_{r}\times\{(x,t):t=-r^{2}\})

as the so-called parabolic boundary of QrQ_{r}.

Proposition 2.5 (Boundary estimates).

Let u∈C⁡(Q¯1)u\in C(\overline{Q}_{1}) be a solution of (2.1) satisfying (2.2). Let φ:=u|∂pQ1\varphi:=u|_{\partial_{p}Q_{1}} and let ρ\rho be a modulus of continuity of φ\varphi. Then there exists another modulus of continuity ρ∗\rho^{*} depending only on n,λ,Λ,ρ,‖φ‖L∞​(∂pQ1)n,\lambda,\Lambda,\rho,\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}Q_{1})} such that

|u⁡(x,t)−u⁡(y,s)|≤ρ∗​(|x−y|∨|t−s|)|u(x,t)-u(y,s)|\leq\rho^{*}(|x-y|\vee\sqrt{|t-s|})

for all (x,t),(y,s)∈Q¯1(x,t),(y,s)\in\overline{Q}_{1}.

The above proposition is an adaptation of Proposition 4.14 in [5] for parabolic equations, whose proof will be given in Appendix B.

Another useful result is the W2,δW^{2,\delta} estimate for parabolic equations, which can be found in Theorem 1.9 and Theorem 2.3 of Krylov [30]. Such estimates were first discovered by F.-H. Lin [35] for elliptic equations.

Theorem 2.6 (W2,δW^{2,\delta} estimates).

Let u∈C⁡(Q¯1)∩C2​(Q1)u\in C(\overline{Q}_{1})\cap C^{2}(Q_{1}) be a solution of (2.1) satisfying (2.2). Then there exist two positive constants δ\delta (small) and CC (large), both of which depend only on n,λn,\lambda and Λ\Lambda, such that

‖∇u‖Lδ​(Q1)+‖∇2u‖Lδ​(Q1)≤C​‖u‖L∞​(∂pQ1).\|\nabla u\|_{L^{\delta}(Q_{1})}+\|\nabla^{2}u\|_{L^{\delta}(Q_{1})}\leq C\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}Q_{1})}.

The last one we will use in this paper is a regularity estimate for small perturbation solutions of fully nonlinear parabolic equations, which was proved by Wang [52]. Such estimates were first proved by Savin [46] for fully nonlinear elliptic equations.

Theorem 2.7 (Regularity of small perturbation solutions).

Let uu be a smooth solution of (2.3) in Q1Q_{1}. For each γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), there exist two positive constants η\eta (small) and CC (large), both of which depends only on γ,n\gamma,n and pp, such that if |u⁡(x,t)−L⁡(x)|≤η|u(x,t)-L(x)|\leq\eta in Q1Q_{1} for some linear function LL of xx satisfying 1/2≤|∇L|≤21/2\leq|\nabla L|\leq 2, then

‖u−L‖C2,γ​(Q1/2)≤C.\|u-L\|_{C^{2,\gamma}(Q_{1/2})}\leq C.
Proof.

Since LL is a solution of (2.3), the conclusion follows from Corollary 1.2 in [52]. ∎

Now let us recall the definition of viscosity solutions to (1.5) (see Definition 2.3 in [1]).

Definition 2.8.

An upper (lower, resp.) semi-continuous function uu in Q1Q_{1} is called a viscosity subsolution (supersolution, resp.) of (1.5) in Q1Q_{1} if for every φ∈C2​(Q1)\varphi\in C^{2}(Q_{1}), u−φu-\varphi has a local maximum (minimum, resp.) at (x0,t0)∈Q1(x_{0},t_{0})\in Q_{1}, then

φt≤(≥,resp.)Δφ+(p−2)|∇φ|−2φiφjφi​j\varphi_{t}\leq(\geq,resp.)\Delta\varphi+(p-2)|\nabla\varphi|^{-2}\varphi_{i}\varphi_{j}\varphi_{ij}

at (x0,t0)(x_{0},t_{0}) when ∇φ​(x0,t0)≠0\nabla\varphi(x_{0},t_{0})\neq 0, and

φt≤(≥,resp.)Δφ+(p−2)qiqjφi​j\varphi_{t}\leq(\geq,resp.)\Delta\varphi+(p-2)q_{i}q_{j}\varphi_{ij}

for some q∈B¯1⊂ℝnq\in\overline{B}_{1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} at (x0,t0)(x_{0},t_{0}) when ∇φ​(x0,t0)=0\nabla\varphi(x_{0},t_{0})=0.

A function u∈C⁡(Q1)u\in C(Q_{1}) is called a viscosity solution of (1.5), if it is both a viscosity subsolution and a viscosity supersolution.

In order to circumvent the inconveniences of the lack of smoothness of viscosity solutions, we choose to approximate the equation (1.5) with a regularized problem. For ε>0\varepsilon>0, let uu be smooth and satisfy that

ut=ai​j​(∇u)​ui​jin ​Q1,u_{t}=a_{ij}(\nabla u)u_{ij}\quad\mbox{in }Q_{1}, (2.3)

where

ai​j​(q)=δi​j+(p−2)​qi​qj|q|2+ε2for ​q∈ℝn.a_{ij}(q)=\delta_{ij}+(p-2)\frac{q_{i}q_{j}}{|q|^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}}\quad\mbox{for }q\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. (2.4)

This equation (2.3) is uniformly parabolic and has smooth solutions for all ε>0\varepsilon>0. Such regularization techniques have been used before for the pp-Laplace equation in several contexts. For example, see [1, 17, 34]. We will obtain a priori estimates that are independent of ε\varepsilon and finally show that they apply to the original equation (1.5) through approximations.

In the step of approximation, we will use the following two properties on the viscosity solutions of (1.5). The first one is the comparison principle, which can be found in Theorem 3.2 in [1].

Theorem 2.9 (Comparison principle).

Let uu and vv be a viscosity subsolution and a viscosity supersolution of (1.5) in Q1Q_{1}, respectively. If u≤vu\leq v on ∂pQ1\partial_{p}Q_{1}, then u≤vu\leq v in Q¯1\overline{Q}_{1}.

The second one is the stability of viscosity solutions of (1.5).

Theorem 2.10 (Stability).

Let {uk}\{u_{k}\} be a sequence of viscosity subsolutions of (2.3) in Q1Q_{1} with εk≥0\varepsilon_{k}\geq 0 that εk→0\varepsilon_{k}\to 0, and uku_{k} converge locally uniformly to uu in Q1Q_{1}. Then uu is a viscosity subsolution of (1.5) in Q1Q_{1}.

Proof.

We refer to the proof of Theorem 2.7 in [17] or the second paragraph of the proof of Theorem 4.2 in [17]. ∎

To summarize, we would like to mention what each of these results in this section will be used for in our proof of Theorem 1.1. The local maximum principle in Theorem 2.2 and the W2,δW^{2,\delta} estimates in Theorem 2.6 will be used to prove Lipschitz estimates. The form of improvement of oscillation in Proposition 2.3, the interior Hölder estimates in Theorem 2.4 and the regularity of small perturbation solutions in Theorem 2.7 are the key ingredients in our proof of the Hölder gradient estimates. The boundary estimates in Proposition 2.5, as well as the comparison principle in Theorem 2.9 and the stability property in Theorem 2.10 will only be used in the technical approximation step, which do not affect the proof of the a priori estimates.

3 Lipschitz estimates in spatial variables

The interior Lipschitz estimate for solutions of (2.3) in spatial variables was essentially obtained before by Does [11]. Here, we will provide an alternative proof. Our proof appears much shorter since it uses Theorem 2.2 and Theorem 2.6, whereas, the proof given by Does [11] is based on the Bernstein technique and uses only elementary tools.

The following auxiliary lemma follows from a direct calculation. We postpone its proof to Appendix A.

Lemma 3.1.

For a smooth solution uu of (2.3) and φ:=(|∇u|2+ε2)p2\varphi:=(|\nabla u|^{2}+\varepsilon^{2})^{\frac{p}{2}} we have

(∂t−ai​j(∇u)∂i​j)φ≤0,\displaystyle\big(\partial_{t}-a_{ij}(\nabla u)\partial_{ij}\big)\varphi\leq 0,

where ai​j​(∇u)a_{ij}(\nabla u) is given in (2.4).

We now present the interior Lipschitz estimate.

Theorem 3.2.

Let uu be a smooth solution of (2.3) in Q1Q_{1}. Then there exists a positive constant CC depending only on nn and pp such that

‖∇u‖L∞​(Q1/2)≤C⁡(‖u‖L∞​(Q1)+ε).\|\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1/2})}\leq C(\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}+\varepsilon).
Proof.

Since uu satisfies (2.3), it follows from Theorem 2.6 that there exist two positive constants δ\delta (small) and CC (large) both of which depend only on nn and pp such that

‖∇u‖Lδ​(Q3/4)≤C​‖u‖L∞​(Q1).\|\nabla u\|_{L^{\delta}(Q_{3/4})}\leq C\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}.

Let φ:=(|∇u|2+ε2)p2\varphi:=(|\nabla u|^{2}+\varepsilon^{2})^{\frac{p}{2}}. By Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 2.2, we have

‖φ‖L∞​(Q1/2)≤C​‖φ‖Lδ/p​(Q3/4)≤C⁡(‖∇u‖Lδ​(Q3/4)p+εp)≤C⁡(‖u‖L∞​(Q1)p+εp).\begin{split}\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1/2})}&\leq C\|\varphi\|_{L^{\delta/p}(Q_{3/4})}\leq C(\|\nabla u\|^{p}_{L^{\delta}(Q_{3/4})}+\varepsilon^{p})\leq C(\|u\|^{p}_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}+\varepsilon^{p}).\end{split}

It follows that

‖∇u‖L∞​(Q1/2)≤C⁡(‖u‖L∞​(Q1)+ε).\|\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1/2})}\leq C(\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}+\varepsilon).

∎

4 Hölder estimates for the spatial gradients

In this section, we shall prove the Hölder estimate of ∇u\nabla u at (0,0)(0,0). By Theorem 3.2 and normalization, we assume that |∇u|≤1|\nabla u|\leq 1. The idea is the following. First, we show that if the projection of ∇u\nabla u onto the direction e∈𝕊n−1e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} is away from 11 in a positive portion of Q1Q_{1}, then ∇u⋅e\nabla u\cdot e has improved oscillation in QτQ_{\tau} for some τ>0\tau>0.

Then we analyze according to the following dichotomy:

  • •

    If we can keep scaling around (0,0)(0,0) and iterate infinitely many times in all directions e∈𝕊n−1e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}, then it leads to the Hölder continuity of ∇u\nabla u at (0,0)(0,0).

  • •

    If the iteration stops at, say, the kk-th step in some direction e∈𝕊n−1e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}. This means that ∇u\nabla u is close to some fixed vector in a large portion of QτkQ_{\tau^{k}}. We then prove that uu is close to some linear function, and the Hölder continuity of ∇u\nabla u will follow from Theorem 2.7.

4.1 Improvement of oscillation

Since ∇u\nabla u is a vector, we shall first obtain an improvement of oscillation for ∇u\nabla u projected to an arbitrary direction e∈𝕊n−1e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}.

Lemma 4.1.

Let uu be a smooth solution of (2.3) such that |∇u|≤1|\nabla u|\leq 1 in Q1Q_{1}. For every 0<ℓ<10<\ell<1, μ>0\mu>0, there exists τ>0\tau>0 depending only on μ\mu and nn, and there exists δ>0\delta>0 depending only on n,p,μn,p,\mu and ℓ\ell such that for arbitrary e∈𝕊n−1e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}, if

|{(x,t)∈Q1:∇u⋅e≤ℓ}|>μ|Q1|,|\{(x,t)\in Q_{1}:\nabla u\cdot e\leq\ell\}|>\mu|Q_{1}|, (4.1)

then

∇u⋅e<1−δin Qτ.\nabla u\cdot e<1-\delta\quad\mbox{in }Q_{\tau}.
Proof.

Let ai​ja_{ij} be as in (2.4), and denote

ai​j,m=∂ai​j∂qm.a_{ij,m}=\frac{\partial a_{ij}}{\partial q_{m}}.

Differentiating (2.3) in xkx_{k}, we have

(uk)t=ai​j​(uk)i​j+ai​j,m​ui​j​(uk)m.(u_{k})_{t}=a_{ij}\big(u_{k})_{ij}+a_{ij,m}u_{ij}(u_{k})_{m}.

Then

(∇u⋅e−ℓ)t=ai​j(∇u⋅e−ℓ)i​j+ai​j,mui​j(∇u⋅e−ℓ)m.(\nabla u\cdot e-\ell)_{t}=a_{ij}\big(\nabla u\cdot e-\ell)_{ij}+a_{ij,m}u_{ij}(\nabla u\cdot e-\ell)_{m}.

Therefore, for

v=|∇u|2,v=|\nabla u|^{2},

we have

vt=ai​j​vi​j+ai​j,m​ui​j​vm−2​ai​j​uk​i​uk​j.v_{t}=a_{ij}v_{ij}+a_{ij,m}u_{ij}v_{m}-2a_{ij}u_{ki}u_{kj}.

For ρ=ℓ/4\rho=\ell/4, let

w=(∇u⋅e−ℓ+ρ|∇u|2)+.w=(\nabla u\cdot e-\ell+\rho|\nabla u|^{2})^{+}.

Then in the region Ω+={(x,t)∈Q1:w>0}\Omega_{+}=\{(x,t)\in Q_{1}:w>0\}, we have

wt=ai​j​wi​j+ai​j,m​ui​j​wm−2​ρ​ai​j​uk​i​uk​j.w_{t}=a_{ij}w_{ij}+a_{ij,m}u_{ij}w_{m}-2\rho a_{ij}u_{ki}u_{kj}.

Since |∇u|>ℓ/2|\nabla u|>\ell/2 in Ω+\Omega_{+}, we have

|ai​j,m|≤4​|p−2|ℓin ​Ω+.|a_{ij,m}|\leq\frac{4|p-2|}{\ell}\quad\mbox{in }\Omega_{+}.

By Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, it follows that

wt≤ai​j​wi​j+c0ρ​ℓ2​|∇w|2in ​Ω+,w_{t}\leq a_{ij}w_{ij}+\frac{c_{0}}{\rho\ell^{2}}|\nabla w|^{2}\quad\mbox{in }\Omega_{+},

for some constant c0>0c_{0}>0 depending only on pp. Therefore, it satisfies in the viscosity sense that

wt≤ai​j​wi​j+c0ρ​ℓ2​|∇w|2in ​Q1.w_{t}\leq a_{ij}w_{ij}+\frac{c_{0}}{\rho\ell^{2}}|\nabla w|^{2}\quad\mbox{in }Q_{1}.

We can choose c1c_{1} such that if we let

and

in the viscosity sense. Since W≥supQ1wW\geq\sup_{Q_{1}}w, then w¯≥0\overline{w}\geq 0 in Q1Q_{1}.

If ∇u⋅e≤ℓ\nabla u\cdot e\leq\ell, then w¯≥(1−eν⁡(ℓ−1))/ν\overline{w}\geq(1-e^{\nu(\ell-1)})/\nu. Therefore, it follows from the assumption that

|{(x,t)∈Q1:w¯≥(1−eν⁡(ℓ−1))/ν}|>μ​|Q1|.|\{(x,t)\in Q_{1}:\overline{w}\geq(1-e^{\nu(\ell-1)})/\nu\}|>\mu|Q_{1}|.

The statement of Lemma 4.1 can be illustrated in Figure 1.

If the condition (4.1) is satisfied in all the directions e∈𝕊n−1e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}, then we obtain the improvement of oscillation for all ∇u⋅e\nabla u\cdot e, which lead to the improvement of oscillation for |∇u||\nabla u|. See Figure 2 and Corollary 4.2.

Corollary 4.2.

Let uu be a smooth solution of (2.3) such that |∇u|≤1|\nabla u|\leq 1 in Q1Q_{1}. For every 0<ℓ<10<\ell<1, μ>0\mu>0, there exist τ∈(0,1/4)\tau\in(0,1/4) depending only on μ\mu and nn, and δ>0\delta>0 depending only on n,p,μ,ℓn,p,\mu,\ell, such that for every nonnegative integer kk, if

|{(x,t)∈Qτi:∇u⋅e≤ℓ(1−δ)i}|>μ|Qτi|for all e∈𝕊n−1 and i=0,⋯,k,|\{(x,t)\in Q_{\tau^{i}}:\nabla u\cdot e\leq\ell(1-\delta)^{i}\}|>\mu|Q_{\tau^{i}}|\quad\mbox{for all }e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\mbox{ and }i=0,\cdots,k, (4.2)

then

|∇u|<(1−δ)i+1in ​Qτi+1​ for all ​i=0,⋯,k.|\nabla u|<(1-\delta)^{i+1}\quad\mbox{in }Q_{\tau^{i+1}}\ \mbox{ for all }i=0,\cdots,k.
Proof.

When i=0i=0, it follows from Lemma 4.1 that ∇u⋅e<1−δ\nabla u\cdot e<1-\delta in QτQ_{\tau} for all e∈𝕊n−1e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}. This implies that |∇u|<1−δ|\nabla u|<1-\delta in QτQ_{\tau}.

Suppose this corollary holds for i=0,⋯,k−1i=0,\cdots,k-1. We are going prove it for i=ki=k. Let

v⁡(x,t)=1τk​(1−δ)k​u​(τk​x,τ2​k​t).v(x,t)=\frac{1}{\tau^{k}(1-\delta)^{k}}u(\tau^{k}x,\tau^{2k}t).

Then vv satisfies

vt=Δ​v+(p−2)​vi​vj|∇v|2+ε​(1−δ)−2​k​vi​jin ​Q1.v_{t}=\Delta v+(p-2)\frac{v_{i}v_{j}}{|\nabla v|^{2}+\varepsilon(1-\delta)^{-2k}}v_{ij}\quad\mbox{in }Q_{1}.

By the induction hypothesis, we also know that |∇v|≤1|\nabla v|\leq 1 in Q1Q_{1}, and

|{(x,t)∈Q1:∇v⋅e≤ℓ}|>μ|Q1|for all e∈𝕊n−1.|\{(x,t)\in Q_{1}:\nabla v\cdot e\leq\ell\}|>\mu|Q_{1}|\quad\mbox{for all }e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}.

Therefore, by Lemma 4.1 we have

∇v⋅e≤1−δin Qτfor all e∈𝕊n−1.\nabla v\cdot e\leq 1-\delta\quad\mbox{in }Q_{\tau}\quad\mbox{for all }e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}.

Hence, |∇v|≤1−δ|\nabla v|\leq 1-\delta in QτQ_{\tau}. Consequently,

|∇u|<(1−δ)k+1in ​Qτk+1.|\nabla u|<(1-\delta)^{k+1}\quad\mbox{in }Q_{\tau^{k+1}}.

∎

4.2 Using the small oscillation

Unless |∇u​(0,0)|=0|\nabla u(0,0)|=0, the condition in (4.2) will fail to be satisfied after finitely many steps of scaling in some direction e∈𝕊n−1e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}, in which we will then show that uu is close to some linear function so that Theorem 2.7 can be applied. See Lemma 4.4 and Figure 3.

Before that, we need a lemma which states that for a solution of a uniformly parabolic linear equation, if its oscillation in space is uniformly small in every time slice, then its oscillation in the space-time is also small.

Lemma 4.3.

Let u∈C⁡(Q¯1)u\in C(\overline{Q}_{1}) be a solution of (2.1) satisfying (2.2) and AA is a positive constant. Assume that for all t∈[−1,0]t\in[-1,0], we have

 oscB1​u​(⋅,t)≤A,\mbox{ osc}_{B_{1}}u(\cdot,t)\leq A,

then

 oscQ1​u≤C​A,\mbox{ osc}_{Q_{1}}u\leq CA,

where CC is a positive constant depending only on Λ\Lambda and the dimension nn.

Proof.

Let w¯​(x,t)=a¯+5​n​Λ​A​t+2​A​|x|2\overline{w}(x,t)=\overline{a}+5n\Lambda At+2A|x|^{2}, where aa is chosen so that w¯​(⋅,−1)≥u⁡(⋅,−1)\overline{w}(\cdot,-1)\geq u(\cdot,-1) and w¯​(x¯,−1)=u⁡(x¯,−1)\overline{w}(\bar{x},-1)=u(\bar{x},-1) for some x¯∈B¯1\bar{x}\in\overline{B}_{1}. If x¯∈∂B1\bar{x}\in\partial B_{1}, then

2A=w¯(x¯,−1)−w¯(0,−1)≤u(x¯,−1)−u(0,−1)≤ oscB1u(⋅−1)≤A,2A=\overline{w}(\bar{x},-1)-\overline{w}(0,-1)\leq u(\bar{x},-1)-u(0,-1)\leq\mbox{ osc}_{B_{1}}u(\cdot-1)\leq A,

which is impossible. Therefore, x¯∈B1\bar{x}\in B_{1}.

We claim that

w¯≥uin ​Q1.\overline{w}\geq u\quad\text{in }Q_{1}.

If not, let m=−infQ1(w¯−u)>0m=-\inf_{Q_{1}}(\overline{w}-u)>0 and (x0,t0)∈Q¯1(x_{0},t_{0})\in\overline{Q}_{1} be such that m=u⁡(x0,t0)−w¯​(x0,t0)m=u(x_{0},t_{0})-\overline{w}(x_{0},t_{0}). By the choice of a¯\bar{a}, we know that t0>−1t_{0}>-1. Since w¯+m≥u\overline{w}+m\geq u in Q1Q_{1}, w¯​(x0,t0)+m=u⁡(x0,t0)\overline{w}(x_{0},t_{0})+m=u(x_{0},t_{0}) and  oscB1​u​(⋅,t0)≤A\mbox{ osc}_{B_{1}}u(\cdot,t_{0})\leq A, by the same reason in the above, we have x0∈B1x_{0}\in B_{1}. Therefore, we have that

(w¯+m)t−ai​j​(x,t)​∂i​j(w¯+m)≤0at ​(x0,t0).(\overline{w}+m)_{t}-a_{ij}(x,t)\partial_{ij}(\overline{w}+m)\leq 0\quad\text{at }(x_{0},t_{0}).

This leads to

5​n​Λ​A≤4​A⋅T​r​(ai​j)≤4​n​Λ​A,5n\Lambda A\leq 4A\cdot Tr(a_{ij})\leq 4n\Lambda A,

which is impossible. This proves the claim.

Similarly, one can show that for w¯​(x,t)=a¯−5​n​Λ​A​t−2​A​|x|2\underline{w}(x,t)=\underline{a}-5n\Lambda At-2A|x|^{2}, we have

w¯≤uin ​Q1,\underline{w}\leq u\quad\text{in }Q_{1},

where a¯\underline{a} is chosen so that w¯​(⋅,−1)≤u⁡(⋅,−1)\underline{w}(\cdot,-1)\leq u(\cdot,-1) and w¯​(x¯,−1)=u⁡(x¯,−1)\underline{w}(\underline{x},-1)=u(\underline{x},-1) for some x¯∈B1\underline{x}\in B_{1}.

Meanwhile, since

w¯​(x¯,−1)−w¯​(x¯,−1)=u⁡(x¯,−1)−u⁡(x¯,−1)≤o​s​cB1​u​(⋅,−1)≤A,\overline{w}(\bar{x},-1)-\underline{w}(\underline{x},-1)=u(\bar{x},-1)-u(\underline{x},-1)\leq osc_{B_{1}}u(\cdot,-1)\leq A,

we have

a¯−a¯≤(10​n​Λ+1)​A.\bar{a}-\underline{a}\leq(10n\Lambda+1)A.

Therefore, we have

 oscQ1​u≤supQ1w¯−infQ1w¯≤a¯−a¯+4​A=(10​n​Λ+5)​A.\mbox{ osc}_{Q_{1}}u\leq\sup_{Q_{1}}\overline{w}-\inf_{Q_{1}}\underline{w}\leq\bar{a}-\underline{a}+4A=(10n\Lambda+5)A.

Lemma 4.4.

Let η\eta be a positive constant and uu be a smooth solution of (2.1) satisfying (2.2). Assume |∇u|≤1|\nabla u|\leq 1 everywhere and

|{(x,t)∈Q1:|∇u−e|>ε0}|≤ε1\left|\left\{(x,t)\in Q_{1}:|\nabla u-e|>\varepsilon_{0}\right\}\right|\leq\varepsilon_{1}

for some e∈𝕊n−1e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} and two positive constants ε0,ε1.\varepsilon_{0},\varepsilon_{1}. Then, if ε0\varepsilon_{0} and ε1\varepsilon_{1} are sufficiently small, there exists a constant a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}, such that

|u⁡(x,t)−a−e⋅x|≤η for all ​(x,t)∈Q1/2.|u(x,t)-a-e\cdot x|\leq\eta\quad\text{ for all }(x,t)\in Q_{1/2}.

Here, both ε0\varepsilon_{0} and ε2\varepsilon_{2} depend only on n,λ,Λn,\lambda,\Lambda and η\eta.

Proof.

Let f⁡(t):=|{x∈B1:|∇u​(x,t)−e|>ε0}|f(t):=|\{x\in B_{1}:|\nabla u(x,t)-e|>\varepsilon_{0}\}|. By the assumptions and Fubini’s theorem, we have that ∫−10f⁡(t)​𝑑t≤ε1\int_{-1}^{0}f(t)\mathrm{d}t\leq\varepsilon_{1}. It follows that for E:={t∈(−1,0):f⁡(t)≥ε1}E:=\{t\in(-1,0):f(t)\geq\sqrt{\varepsilon_{1}}\}, we obtain

|E|≤1ε1​∫Ef⁡(t)​𝑑t≤1ε1​∫−10f⁡(t)​𝑑t≤ε1.|E|\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{1}}}\int_{E}f(t)\mathrm{d}t\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{1}}}\int_{-1}^{0}f(t)\mathrm{d}t\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon_{1}}.

Therefore, for all t∈(−1,0]∖Et\in(-1,0]\setminus E, with |E|≤ε1|E|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon_{1}}, we have

|{x∈B1:|∇u​(x,t)−e|>ε0}|≤ε1.|\{x\in B_{1}:|\nabla u(x,t)-e|>\varepsilon_{0}\}|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon_{1}}. (4.3)

It follows from (4.3) and Morrey’s inequality (see, e.g., Section 5.6.2 in the book [13]) that for all t∈(−1,0]∖Et\in(-1,0]\setminus E, we have

 oscB1/2​(u⁡(⋅,t)−e⋅x)≤C⁡(n)​‖∇u−e‖L2​n​(B1)≤C⁡(n)​(ε0+ε114​n),\mbox{ osc}_{B_{1/2}}(u(\cdot,t)-e\cdot x)\leq C(n)\|\nabla u-e\|_{L^{2n}(B_{1})}\leq C(n)(\varepsilon_{0}+\varepsilon_{1}^{\frac{1}{4n}}), (4.4)

where C⁡(n)>0C(n)>0 depends only on nn.

Meanwhile, since |∇u|≤1|\nabla u|\leq 1 in Q1Q_{1}, we have that  oscB1​u​(⋅,t)≤2\mbox{ osc}_{B_{1}}u(\cdot,t)\leq 2 for all t∈(−1,0]t\in(-1,0]. Thus, applying Lemma 4.3, we have that  oscQ1​u≤C\mbox{ osc}_{Q_{1}}u\leq C for some constant CC. The function uu is a solution of a uniformly parabolic equation. By Theorem 2.4, we have

‖u‖Cα​(Q1/2)≤C\|u\|_{C^{\alpha}(Q_{1/2})}\leq C

for some positive constants α\alpha and CC depending only on λ,Λ,n\lambda,\Lambda,n. Therefore, by (4.4) and the fact that |E|≤ε1|E|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon_{1}}, we obtain

 oscB1/2​(u⁡(⋅,t)−e⋅x)≤C⁡(ε0+ε114​n+ε1α4)\mbox{ osc}_{B_{1/2}}(u(\cdot,t)-e\cdot x)\leq C(\varepsilon_{0}+\varepsilon_{1}^{\frac{1}{4n}}+\varepsilon_{1}^{\frac{\alpha}{4}})

for all t∈(−1/4,0]t\in(-1/4,0] (that is, including t∈Et\in E). By Lemma 4.3, we obtain

where C>0C>0 depends only on λ,Λ,n\lambda,\Lambda,n. Hence, if ε0\varepsilon_{0} and ε1\varepsilon_{1} are sufficiently small, there exists a constant a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}, such that

|u⁡(t,x)−a−e⋅x|≤η for all ​(x,t)∈Q1/2.|u(t,x)-a-e\cdot x|\leq\eta\quad\text{ for all }(x,t)\in Q_{1/2}.

4.3 Iteration

In this section, we finish our proof of the following a priori estimates.

Theorem 4.5.

Let uu be a smooth solution of (2.3) in Q1Q_{1}. Then there exist two positive constants α\alpha and CC depending only on nn and pp such that

‖∇u‖Cα​(Q1/2)≤C⁡(‖u‖L∞​(Q1)+ε).\|\nabla u\|_{C^{\alpha}(Q_{1/2})}\leq C(\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}+\varepsilon).

Also, there holds

sup(x,t),(x,s)∈Q1/2|u⁡(x,t)−u⁡(x,s)||t−s|1+α2≤C⁡(‖u‖L∞​(Q1)+ε).\sup_{(x,t),(x,s)\in Q_{1/2}}\frac{|u(x,t)-u(x,s)|}{|t-s|^{\frac{1+\alpha}{2}}}\leq C(\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}+\varepsilon).
Proof.

We first show the Hölder estimate of ∇u\nabla u at (0,0)(0,0). Moreover, by normalization, we may assume that u⁡(0,0)=0u(0,0)=0 and |∇u|≤1|\nabla u|\leq 1 in Q1Q_{1}.

Let η\eta be the one in Theorem 2.7 with γ=1/2\gamma=1/2, and for this η\eta, let ε0,ε1\varepsilon_{0},\varepsilon_{1} be two sufficiently small positive constants so that the conclusion of Lemma 4.4 holds. For ℓ=1−ε02/2\ell=1-\varepsilon_{0}^{2}/2 and μ=ε1/|Q1|\mu=\varepsilon_{1}/|Q_{1}|, if

|{(x,t)∈Q1:∇u⋅e≤ℓ}|≤μ|Q1|for any e∈𝕊n−1,|\{(x,t)\in Q_{1}:\nabla u\cdot e\leq\ell\}|\leq\mu|Q_{1}|\quad\mbox{for any }e\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1},

then

|{(x,t)∈Q1:|∇u−e|>ε0}|≤ε1.\left|\left\{(x,t)\in Q_{1}:|\nabla u-e|>\varepsilon_{0}\right\}\right|\leq\varepsilon_{1}.

This is because if |∇u​(x,t)−e|>ε0|\nabla u(x,t)-e|>\varepsilon_{0} for some (x,t)∈Q1(x,t)\in Q_{1}, then

|∇u|2−2∇u⋅e+1≥ε02.|\nabla u|^{2}-2\nabla u\cdot e+1\geq\varepsilon_{0}^{2}.

Since |∇u|≤1|\nabla u|\leq 1, we have

∇u⋅e≤1−ε02/2.\nabla u\cdot e\leq 1-\varepsilon_{0}^{2}/2.

Therefore, if ℓ=1−ε02/2\ell=1-\varepsilon_{0}^{2}/2 and μ=ε1/|Q1|\mu=\varepsilon_{1}/|Q_{1}|, then

{(x,t)∈Q1:|∇u−e|>ε0}⊂{(x,t)∈Q1:∇u⋅e≤ℓ},\left\{(x,t)\in Q_{1}:|\nabla u-e|>\varepsilon_{0}\right\}\subset\{(x,t)\in Q_{1}:\nabla u\cdot e\leq\ell\},

from which it follows that

5 Approximations and the proof of our main result

This section is devoted to the final step of our proof of Theorem 1.1, that is the approximation step.

Note that (2.3) is a uniformly parabolic quasilinear equation and its coefficients ai​j​(q)a_{ij}(q) as in (2.4) are smooth with bounded derivatives (for each value of ε>0\varepsilon>0). The next lemma follows directly from classical quasilinear equations theory (see, e.g., Theorem 4.4 of [32] in page 560) and the Schauder estimates.

Lemma 5.1.

Let g∈C⁡(∂pQ1)g\in C(\partial_{p}Q_{1}). For ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a unique solution uε∈C∞​(Q1)∩C⁡(Q¯1)u^{\varepsilon}\in C^{\infty}(Q_{1})\cap C(\overline{Q}_{1}) of (2.3) such that uε=gu^{\varepsilon}=g on ∂pQ1\partial_{p}Q_{1}.

We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.1 by taking ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 in the a priori estimate of Theorem 4.5.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Without loss of generality, we assume that u∈C⁡(Q¯1)u\in C(\overline{Q}_{1}). Let ω\omega be its modulus of continuity in Q¯1\overline{Q}_{1}. By Lemma 5.1, for ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), there exists a unique solution vε∈C∞​(Q1)∩C⁡(Q¯1)v^{\varepsilon}\in C^{\infty}(Q_{1})\cap C(\overline{Q}_{1}) of (2.3) such that vε=uv^{\varepsilon}=u on ∂pQ1\partial_{p}Q_{1}. Moreover, it follows from Theorem 2.5 that there exists a modulus of continuity ω∗\omega^{*}, which depends only on n,p,ω,‖u‖L∞​(∂pQ1)n,p,\omega,\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}Q_{1})}, such that

|vε​(x,t)−vε​(y,s)|≤ω∗​(|x−y|∨|s−t|) for all ​(x,t),(y,s)∈Q¯1.|v^{\varepsilon}(x,t)-v^{\varepsilon}(y,s)|\leq\omega^{*}(|x-y|\vee\sqrt{|s-t|})\quad\mbox{ for all }(x,t),(y,s)\in\overline{Q}_{1}.

By the maximum principle,

‖vε‖L∞​(Q1)≤‖u‖L∞​(∂pQ1).\|v^{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}\leq\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}Q_{1})}.

It follows from Ascoli-Arzela theorem that there exists a subsequence {vεk}\{v^{\varepsilon_{k}}\} such that vεk→v∈C⁡(Q¯1)v^{\varepsilon_{k}}\to v\in C(\overline{Q}_{1}) uniformly in Q¯1\overline{Q}_{1} as εk→0\varepsilon_{k}\to 0. By the stability property in Theorem 2.10, vv is a viscosity solution of (1.5). By the comparison principle in Theorem 2.9, we obtain that u≡vu\equiv v in Q¯1\overline{Q}_{1}.

On the other hand, it follows from Theorem 4.5 that, subject to a subsequence, ∇vεk\nabla v^{\varepsilon_{k}} converges in Cα​(Q1/2)C^{\alpha}(Q_{1/2}) for some constant α\alpha depending only on nn and pp. Therefore, uu is differentiable in xx everywhere in Q1/2Q_{1/2}, and thus, ∇vεk\nabla v^{\varepsilon_{k}} converges to ∇u\nabla u in Cα​(Q1/2)C^{\alpha}(Q_{1/2}). Since

‖∇vεk‖Cα​(Q1/2)≤C⁡(‖vεk‖L∞​(Q1)+εk)≤C⁡(‖u‖L∞​(Q1)+εk),\|\nabla v^{\varepsilon_{k}}\|_{C^{\alpha}(Q_{1/2})}\leq C(\|v^{\varepsilon_{k}}\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}+\varepsilon_{k})\leq C(\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}+\varepsilon_{k}),

where C>0C>0 depends only on nn and pp, we obtain

‖∇u‖Cα​(Q1/2)≤C​‖u‖L∞​(Q1)\|\nabla u\|_{C^{\alpha}(Q_{1/2})}\leq C\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}

by sending k→∞k\to\infty.

We also know from Theorem 4.5 that for all (x,t),(x,s)∈Q1/2(x,t),(x,s)\in Q_{1/2}, there holds

|vεk​(x,t)−vεk​(x,s)|≤C⁡(‖u‖L∞​(Q1)+εk)​|t−s|1+α2.|v^{\varepsilon_{k}}(x,t)-v^{\varepsilon_{k}}(x,s)|\leq C(\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}+\varepsilon_{k})|t-s|^{\frac{1+\alpha}{2}}.

By sending k→∞k\to\infty, we obtain

sup(x,t),(x,s)∈Q1/2|u⁡(x,t)−u⁡(x,s)||t−s|1+α2≤C​‖u‖L∞​(Q1).\sup_{(x,t),(x,s)\in Q_{1/2}}\frac{|u(x,t)-u(x,s)|}{|t-s|^{\frac{1+\alpha}{2}}}\leq C\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}.

This finishes the proof of Theorem 1.1. ∎

where ρ¯\overline{\rho} is a modulus continuity of ψ\psi. Therefore, we have for (y,s)∈B¯1×[−1,t](y,s)\in\overline{B}_{1}\times[-1,t],

|u⁡(x,t)−u⁡(y,s)|≤ρ⁡(3​r)+2​‖u‖L∞​(∂pQ1)​ρ¯​((|x−y|∨|t−s|)/r).|u(x,t)-u(y,s)|\leq\rho(3r)+2\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}Q_{1})}\overline{\rho}((|x-y|\vee\sqrt{|t-s|})/r).

The conclusion then follows from the observation that

ρ∗​(d)=infr∈(0,1)(ρ⁡(3​r)+2​‖u‖L∞​(∂pQ1)​ρ¯​(d/r))\rho^{*}(d)=\inf_{r\in(0,1)}\left(\rho(3r)+2\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}Q_{1})}\overline{\rho}(d/r)\right)

is a modulus of continuity. ∎

Lemma B.3.

Let t∈[−1,0)t\in[-1,0) and u∈C⁡(B¯1×[t,0])u\in C(\overline{B}_{1}\times[t,0]) be a solution of (2.1) in B1×(t,0]B_{1}\times(t,0] satisfying (2.2). Let x∈B¯1x\in\overline{B}_{1} be fixed, ρ\rho be a modulus of continuity such that

|u⁡(y,s)−u⁡(x,t)|≤ρ⁡(|x−y|∨|s−t|)|u(y,s)-u(x,t)|\leq\rho(|x-y|\vee\sqrt{|s-t|})

for all (y,s)∈∂p(B1×(t,0])(y,s)\in\partial_{p}(B_{1}\times(t,0]). Then there exists another modulus of continuity ρ∗\rho^{*} depending only on n,λ,Λ,ρn,\lambda,\Lambda,\rho and ‖u‖L∞​(∂p(B1×(t,0]))\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}(B_{1}\times(t,0]))} such that

Then

vs−ai​j​vi​j≥0in ​B1×(t,0].v_{s}-a_{ij}v_{ij}\geq 0\quad\mbox{in }B_{1}\times(t,0].

For (y,s)∈∂p(B1×(t,0])(y,s)\in\partial_{p}(B_{1}\times(t,0]) and |y−x|∨|s−t|<r|y-x|\vee\sqrt{|s-t|}<r, then

For (y,s)∈∂p(B1×(t,0])(y,s)\in\partial_{p}(B_{1}\times(t,0]) and |y−x|∨|s−t|≥r|y-x|\vee\sqrt{|s-t|}\geq r, then either |y−x|≥r|y-x|\geq r or |s−t|≥r2|s-t|\geq r^{2}, each of which implies that

v⁡(y,s)≥u⁡(x,t)+2​‖u‖L∞​(∂p(B1×(t,0]))=u⁡(x,t)+2​‖u‖L∞​(B1×(t,0])≥u⁡(y,s).v(y,s)\geq u(x,t)+2\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}(B_{1}\times(t,0]))}=u(x,t)+2\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(B_{1}\times(t,0])}\geq u(y,s).

It follows from the maximum principle that v≥uv\geq u in Q¯1\overline{Q}_{1}, i.e.,

ρ⁡(r)+2​‖u‖L∞​(∂p(B1×(t,0]))​ϕ​(y−xr,s−tr2)≥u⁡(y,s)−u⁡(x,t).\rho(r)+2\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}(B_{1}\times(t,0]))}\phi\Big(\frac{y-x}{r},\frac{s-t}{r^{2}}\Big)\geq u(y,s)-u(x,t).

ρ⁡(r)+2​‖u‖L∞​(∂p(B1×(t,0]))​ϕ​(y−xr,s−tr2)≥u⁡(x,t)−u⁡(y,s).\rho(r)+2\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}(B_{1}\times(t,0]))}\phi\Big(\frac{y-x}{r},\frac{s-t}{r^{2}}\Big)\geq u(x,t)-u(y,s).

Lemma B.4.

Let u∈C⁡(Q¯1)u\in C(\overline{Q}_{1}) be a solution of (2.1) satisfying (2.2). Let (x,t)∈∂B1×(−1,0](x,t)\in\partial B_{1}\times(-1,0] be fixed, ρ\rho be a modulus of continuity such that

for all (y,s)∈Q¯1(y,s)\in\overline{Q}_{1}.

for all (y,s)∈B¯1×[−1,t](y,s)\in\overline{B}_{1}\times[-1,t]. If t<0t<0, by applying Lemma B.3 to the cylinder B1×(t,0)B_{1}\times(t,0) and noticing that ‖u‖L∞​(∂p(B1×(t,0]))≤‖u‖L∞​(Q1)≤‖u‖L∞​(∂pQ1)\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}(B_{1}\times(t,0]))}\leq\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{1})}\leq\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}Q_{1})}, we conclude that there exists a modulus of continuity ρ2\rho_{2} depending only on n,λ,Λ,ρ,‖u‖L∞​(∂pQ1)n,\lambda,\Lambda,\rho,\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\partial_{p}Q_{1})} such that

Corollary B.5.

Let u∈C⁡(Q¯1)u\in C(\overline{Q}_{1}) be a solution of (2.1) satisfying (2.2). Let (x,t)∈∂pQ1(x,t)\in\partial_{p}Q_{1} be fixed, ρ\rho be a modulus of continuity such that

|u⁡(y,s)−u⁡(x,t)|≤ρ⁡(|x−y|∨|t−s|)|u(y,s)-u(x,t)|\leq\rho(|x-y|\vee\sqrt{|t-s|})

for all (y,s)∈Q¯1(y,s)\in\overline{Q}_{1}.

It follows from Lemma B.3 and Lemma B.4. ∎

ρ1​(d):=C​supm≥1ρ~​(2m+2​d)2m​α\rho_{1}(d):=C\sup_{m\geq 1}\frac{\tilde{\rho}(2^{m+2}d)}{2^{m\alpha}}

If (y,s)∉BdX/2(x)×(t−dX2/4,t](y,s)\not\in B_{d_{X}/2}(x)\times(t-d_{X}^{2}/4,t], then
